A real measurable function admits uniform approximation by finite-valued simple functions ex-

error; an unbounded function cannot be uniformly close to even one finite-valued function.

question.text:
Let f be a real measurable function on a nonempty set with a sigma algebra. Which condition
is equivalent to the existence of finite-valued measurable simple functions converging uniformly
to f?
(A) f is bounded.
(B) f is nonnegative.
(C) f has countable range.
(D) f is integrable.
(E) f vanishes outside a set of finite measure.

solution.text:
Every finite-valued simple function is bounded. If s → f uniformly, choose one s with
n n
sup |s − f| < 1; then f is bounded. Conversely, for bounded measurable f , rounding its
n
values down to multiples of 1/n produces a finite-valued measurable function with error
less than 1/n. The range bound, rather than the size of the underlying domain, is decisive.
